solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: This time the game is not in the bag!

definitions.text: This time the game is not in the bag!

parts.words: This time the game is not in the bag!
parts.note: surface reading: a moment when a contest's result is still far from certain

parts.words: the game is not in the bag
parts.note: setter's reading: game means hunted animals and birds, which may not legally be shot and bagged in this period

explanation.surface: A sports fan warns that the match is far from won yet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the bag' sounds like a sporting certainty, but game here is quarry for hunters, and the bag is what the shooter carries home.
explanation.definitionFit: The months when hunting particular animals or fish is forbidden by law are named this, so nothing gets bagged.

clue.text: Put the left hand on

indicators.note: in a down clue, one thing placed on another sits below it, so the second word follows the first

parts.note: standard abbreviation for left
a hand is help, as in 'give me a hand'

explanation.surface: An instruction to place your left hand on something, perhaps a Bible for an oath.
explanation.definitionFit: Past tense of lay, as in 'she laid the book down', which means the same as put in its past form.

clue.text: Shut up when taken into the band

indicators.note: something taken into another thing ends up held within it

parts.note: the hushing sound telling someone to be quiet
as in 'as I left' meaning 'when I left'

explanation.surface: Someone told to be quiet once they join the musical group.
explanation.walkthrough: Band looks like a group of musicians; it is a strip of cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: A sash is a long strip of fabric worn round the waist or over a shoulder, a kind of band.

clue.text: Told on pop. Misbehaving in the outhouse

indicators.note: one part is placed inside the outer building word

parts.note: a shed is a small outbuilding

indicators.note: letters that misbehave will not stay in their proper places

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A child reports their father for some mischief in the garden shed.
explanation.walkthrough: Pop reads as father, but it is just three letters to be jumbled. To shop someone is British slang for informing on them to the police.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang, informing against a person to the authorities is shopping them, so told on matches the past tense.

clue.text: The crack about height hurt

indicators.note: one word goes around another, enclosing it

parts.note: a crack shot or player is an expert, an ace
standard abbreviation for height

explanation.surface: A wisecrack about someone's height wounded them.
explanation.walkthrough: Crack suggests a joke, but here it is the adjective for a top performer.
explanation.definitionFit: To ache is to suffer a dull persistent pain, so it works as the verb hurt.

clue.text: Book by which the reader gets carried away?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a volume collecting several works by one author

definitions.text: by which the reader gets carried away?
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a public road vehicle that transports passengers, who may be reading on it

explanation.surface: A gripping novel that sweeps its reader away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carried away' suggests being enthralled; the question mark warns it is meant literally, as a passenger on old-fashioned public transport.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a single volume gathering several works, and is also the original full name for a bus.

clue.text: Blood shot again

parts.note: a shot is an attempt, a go
the prefix meaning again, as in redo

explanation.surface: Bloodshot eyes once more, perhaps after another late night.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface runs blood and shot together as bloodshot; they must be split.
explanation.definitionFit: Gore is spilled, often clotted, blood from a wound, as in a gory film.

clue.text: It's misery when the devil makes his home among us

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an utterly wretched situation

definitions.text: when the devil makes his home among us
definitions.meaning: second meaning, read literally: Satan's underworld relocated to the world where people live

explanation.surface: A gloomy observation that life is wretched when evil lives among us.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes an utterly miserable place or experience, literally the underworld transplanted to our world.

clue.text: Single — and a catch

definitions.meaning: first meaning: only, one and alone
second meaning: a flatfish an angler might land

explanation.surface: A personal ad: unattached and quite a catch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A catch' suggests a desirable partner; here it is something caught by a fisherman.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means only or unique, as in sole heir, and also names a flat fish often caught and eaten.

clue.text: Be a good looker but no beauty competition winner

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to be observant, noticing every detail
second meaning: read as a pageant title, a Miss of something worthless

explanation.surface: Someone attractive who still never wins a beauty pageant.
explanation.walkthrough: A good looker sounds like an attractive person, but it means a keen observer. Beauty queens take titles like Miss World.
explanation.definitionFit: An observant person notices every detail, and a pageant winner styled Miss followed by a zero title has won nothing.

clue.text: The male will, you say, stay close by

indicators.note: what you say is heard rather than seen written down

parts.note: the man will, contracted

explanation.surface: A man promising to stay nearby.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the command to a dog to walk close beside its owner.
explanation.definitionFit: The dog-training command tells the animal to keep close behind or beside the handler's foot.

clue.text: Tell nobody the answer to 'Palindromic relation'

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the idiom asking someone to keep a secret
second meaning: a clue within a clue, whose solution is a word for mother that reads the same both ways

explanation.surface: Keep quiet about the solution to a crossword clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The inner clue's solution is a three-letter word for mother, and the phrase states that this is the word.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is a request for silence, said when something must stay secret among those who know.

clue.text: There's a passage about Art Nouveau. It's unintelligible

indicators.note: one set of letters goes around the other
French for new, so the word beside it is given a new form

parts.note: taken as written without the apostrophe, also rearranged

indicators.note: a muddled string of letters cannot be understood, so it must be sorted out

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A critic says a passage of writing about Art Nouveau makes no sense.
explanation.walkthrough: Passage seems to be text, but it is a channel of water; Art Nouveau looks like the art movement, yet it is two separate words.
explanation.definitionFit: A strait is a narrow channel of sea joining two larger bodies of water, a passage for ships.

clue.text: Turned out the one inside is new

indicators.note: one piece goes within the others
letters put out of order are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: It turns out the person inside is a newcomer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned out' reads as 'proved to be', but it is the word to jumble plus its signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Something not yet tested or tried out is new and inexperienced, like an untested recruit.

clue.text: "Mother's gone mad and her sister" does frighten

indicators.note: the word for mother has gone, so it is taken away from the following word

parts.note: an informal word for mother
taken as written
a mother's sister is the child's aunt

explanation.surface: A frightening family scene: mother has lost her mind, and so has her sister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gone mad' looks like a phrase meaning insane; instead the letters of mother are removed from mad, leaving only its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To daunt someone is to intimidate or dishearten them, which is close to frightening them.

clue.text: Stops and arrests

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a vehicle drawing over to the side of the road
second meaning: police taking a suspect into custody

explanation.surface: A police report: the officer stops a driver and arrests them.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb describes a car or train halting at the roadside or station, and police bringing in a suspect.

clue.text: They're very high, for the hearing of dogs

indicators.note: the words are meant for the ear, so the answer only sounds like them

parts.note: mountain summits are very high

explanation.surface: A note that dogs can hear very high-pitched sounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very high' suggests a dog whistle's pitch; it is mountain tops. A Peke is short for Pekinese, a small toy dog breed.
explanation.definitionFit: Pekes are Pekinese, small flat-faced toy dogs originally bred in China, so they are examples of dogs.

clue.text: A race that has its supporters

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a horse race with a prize funded by the owners' entry money
second meaning: wooden posts that hold up plants or fences

explanation.surface: A contest that draws plenty of fans.
explanation.walkthrough: Supporters suggest fans cheering; here they are posts holding plants up.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a type of horse race with prize money, and is the plural of posts driven into ground for support.

clue.text: Making the foreigners pronounce "condescends"

indicators.note: pronouncing a word gives its sound, not its spelling

parts.note: to condescend is to deign, stoop to do something

explanation.surface: Snooty foreigners made to say a long English word.
explanation.walkthrough: Danes are people from Denmark, foreigners to the British setter.
explanation.definitionFit: Natives of Denmark are, from the British point of view, a particular group of foreign people.

clue.text: Holding a pen as a prop

indicators.note: something holding another thing has it inside

parts.note: a pen for pigs
taken as written

explanation.surface: An actor using a pen as a stage prop.
explanation.walkthrough: Pen looks like a writing tool and prop like a theatre object; they are an animal enclosure and a support.
explanation.definitionFit: A stay is a brace or rope that supports something, such as a mast, so it is a prop.

clue.text: Dad, at half past, starts packing

indicators.note: only half the word is kept, the rest dropped

parts.note: taken as written, then cut in half

indicators.note: the beginning letters of the word are taken

parts.note: its opening pair of letters

explanation.surface: At half past, father begins to pack his bags.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half past' looks like a time; it means the first half of past. Starts here takes the first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a familiar, somewhat old-fashioned word children use for their father.

clue.text: Resentful to start off with, scoff at

indicators.note: letters that are off are out of their proper order
only the start of the word is used, its ending dropped

parts.note: taken as written, then shortened

explanation.surface: Someone bitter from the outset mocks another person.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the first five letters of resentful are used before they are jumbled.
explanation.definitionFit: To sneer is to show contempt with a mocking expression or remark, much like scoffing at someone.

clue.text: Stopover is about a day in France, child

indicators.note: one word goes around the other

parts.note: a male child
the French word for day

explanation.surface: A traveller's day-long break in France with a child.
explanation.definitionFit: A sojourn is a temporary stay somewhere, much like a stopover on a journey.

clue.text: Cheating in the greenwood

parts.note: green means inexperienced or unripe, raw
deal is timber of pine or fir
the printed compound word, split by the setter into the two pieces above

explanation.surface: Someone up to no good among the trees, like Robin Hood's band.
explanation.walkthrough: Greenwood looks like one word; it splits into green and wood.
explanation.definitionFit: Unfair treatment, in which a person is cheated or done out of their due, is called by this phrase.

clue.text: Photos showing dancing at a tiptop night club

indicators.note: dancing letters move about and change places

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

indicators.note: the top of a down-to-earth word is its first letter

parts.note: read as the top of tip, its leading letter

explanation.surface: Pictures of people dancing at a top-class nightclub.
explanation.walkthrough: Tiptop looks like praise for the club, but it splits into tip and top.
explanation.definitionFit: A lively, fashionable venue for nightlife is commonly called this, so a night club fits.

clue.text: Prominent Arab delegated to go round

indicators.note: one word goes round the other, enclosing it

parts.note: someone delegated is sent on another's behalf
a common Arab man's name

explanation.surface: A leading Arab figure is given the job of making the rounds.
explanation.definitionFit: Salient means most noticeable or important, standing out from the rest, which is prominent.

clue.text: Having the sense to take a hot tip

parts.note: good sense or intelligence, as in having the wit to do something

indicators.note: the tip of a word is its first letter

parts.note: its opening letter

explanation.surface: A punter shrewd enough to back a racing tip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot tip' reads as racing advice; it means the tip of hot.
explanation.definitionFit: With can mean possessing, as in 'a man with a beard', so it stands for the participle having.

clue.text: Ornamentation is in order

definitions.meaning: first meaning: decorative edging on clothes or furniture
second meaning: neat and in good condition

explanation.surface: A tidy decorator's view that decoration is fine.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means decorative edging or detail, and as an adjective it means neat, tidy and well kept.

clue.text: Mountain climbing for a bet

indicators.note: in a down clue, climbing means reading from bottom to top

parts.note: the stake put in before a poker hand

explanation.surface: A wager that someone will climb a mountain.
explanation.walkthrough: Etna is the volcano in Sicily.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the famous active volcano on Sicily, the highest peak in Italy south of the Alps.

clue.text: Reputed to have put out to grass

indicators.note: the letters spelling put are thrown out of the word

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A racehorse said to have been retired to pasture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out to grass' is the idiom for retirement; here put is removed, and grass is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Reeds are tall grasses growing in wetland, so the answer names a kind of grass.

clue.text: Too much duck oil

parts.note: over the top, excessive
a duck in cricket is a score of zero, shaped like O

explanation.surface: Overdoing it with oil when cooking a duck.
explanation.walkthrough: A duck in cricket is a batsman's score of nought.
explanation.definitionFit: Otto, also called attar, is a fragrant essential oil distilled from rose petals.

clue.text: Rewards with only useless land

parts.note: as in 'just one', merely
barren regions where nothing grows

explanation.surface: Someone receives nothing but worthless territory as payment.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a poor reward, which fits: the phrase usually means a deserved punishment.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means what a person truly deserves, usually a fitting punishment, a kind of reward or comeuppance.

clue.text: Pelt I smuggled out

indicators.note: the outer word lies out around the other piece

parts.note: to run goods is to smuggle them
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to smuggling an animal skin out of a country.
explanation.walkthrough: Pelt reads as a fur, but it is the verb for heavy rain beating down.
explanation.definitionFit: To pelt is to fall heavily, as in 'it was pelting down', so a downpour of water drops fits.

clue.text: 'Awaiting delivery' is not necessary

definitions.meaning: first meaning: read literally, a parcel nobody has yet come to collect
second meaning: unwarranted or gratuitous, as of a rude remark

explanation.surface: An official notice saying a package waiting to be sent is unneeded.
explanation.walkthrough: Split in two, the phrase describes goods no one has called for; as one idiom it means uncalled-for.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a remark or action that is unjustified and unneeded, and literally means not yet collected.
